A.P. Moller - Maersk reported a group return on invested capital (ROIC) of 12.3% for 2024 (up from 7.4% in 2023).

- The 12.3% was above the yearly target of above 7.5% under normalised conditions, though profitability lagged in the first half of 2024 before the strong second half brought it above target (Roadmap towards 2025 section).
- The measure is reported as "Return on invested capital after tax (ROIC)" in the five-year summary and financial ratios, calculated on a last-12-months basis (Financial review section).
- The average ROIC over 2021-2024 was 31.3%, well above the 12% target for the 2021-2025 period (Roadmap towards 2025 section).

Lerøy's catch volume fell from 75 893 tonnes (HOG) in 2023 to 64 991 tonnes in 2024 — a drop of about 10 900 tonnes, or roughly 14% (Key figures for the Group; Results and KPI's – WildCatch).

Points behind this and the outlook:
- The decline reflects significant quota cuts: cod quotas were reduced by 34% and haddock by 43% year-on-year, plus a 6% cut in the northern saithe quota (Results and KPI's – WildCatch).
- The quota reductions are to historic low levels and have a negative impact on catch volumes and profitability (CEO's "Optimistic about the times ahead").
- The company expects 2025 and probably 2026 to remain challenging for WildCatch, as earnings are significantly affected by the low quota basis (Market and outlook).
- For 2025, the cod quota falls a further 32% and haddock 2%, while the North Sea/southern saithe quota rises 40%; the trawl ladder's reintroduction cuts Havfisk's cod quota more than the overall decline, and quota redistribution will lead to further job losses in Norway's whitefish industry (Market and outlook).
- The Group continues to focus on improving operational efficiency at sea and onshore, including using frozen raw materials year-round and rebuilding factories (e.g., Båtsfjord and a NOK 150+ million investment in Kjøllefjord) to increase capacity utilisation (Strategic priorities – WildCatch).

The Island - starting point: population of about seven millions, with present produce equal to the support of such a number
The Island - after fifty years (two periods of twenty-five years): population of twenty-eight millions, and the means of subsistence only equal to the support of twenty-one millions

Malthus starts from a population of about seven millions; after fifty years the population would be twenty-eight millions while subsistence would support only twenty-one millions, leaving seven millions unprovided for.

Principal states of modern Europe - 1798: they require three or four hundred years, or more, to double their numbers.
American back settlements - 1798: they doubled their number in fifteen years.

Comparison: 300 ÷ 15 = 20 (or 400 ÷ 15 ≈ 26.7), so the back settlements' population grew roughly 20 to 27 times faster than that of the principal European states.

Darwin credited Malthus, whose Essay on the Principle of Population (1798) states that population, when unchecked, increases in a geometrical ratio, while subsistence increases only in an arithmetical ratio (Chapter 1). As his rule for unchecked population, Malthus takes the doubling every twenty-five years observed in the United States, where means of subsistence were ample and checks to early marriage few (Chapter 2).

The retailer's use is prohibited; the lab's original research use is not caught.

- Recital 25 excludes from the Regulation's scope AI systems specifically developed and put into service for the sole purpose of scientific research and development, so the lab's initial development and use falls outside the Act.
- Recital 44 prohibits placing on the market, putting into service, or using AI systems intended to detect the emotional state of individuals in situations related to the workplace and education, because of the power imbalance and risk of detrimental treatment of workers.
- Recital 44's only exception covers systems placed on the market strictly for medical or safety reasons (e.g. therapeutic use), which does not apply to a retailer monitoring staff mood.
- Recital 24 confirms that a system used for an excluded purpose (research) that is later used for other purposes falls within the scope of the Regulation, so the retailer's deployment is fully covered and prohibited.

The platform must inform the user in a clear and easily comprehensible way of its decision, the reasons for it, and the available possibilities for redress (recital 54). The user can contest the decision through the platform's internal complaint-handling system, which must be easily accessible, lead to swift, non-discriminatory, non-arbitrary and fair outcomes, and involve human review where automated means were used (recital 58). The possibility to lodge a complaint for reversal of the decision must be available for at least six months, calculated from the moment the platform informed the user of the decision (recital 58). The complaint system must not set formal requirements such as referral to specific legal provisions (recital 58). The evidence does not state any cost for using the internal complaint system.

No, the short-term right to reject is no longer available. Under section 22(3), the time limit for exercising it is the end of 30 days beginning with the first day after ownership/possession has been transferred and the goods have been delivered, and the laptop was delivered ten weeks ago.

The next remedy is the right to repair or replacement under section 23: the consumer can require the trader to repair or replace the goods within a reasonable time and without significant inconvenience, at the trader's cost (section 23(2)). If that fails, is impossible or disproportionate, the consumer then has the right to a price reduction or the final right to reject under section 24 (see section 19(3)).

On the burden of proof, the consumer does not have to prove the fault existed at delivery: under section 19(14), goods which do not conform at any time within six months of delivery must be taken not to have conformed on the day of delivery, unless the trader establishes that they did conform (section 19(15)).
